title: Testing Whether Concept Erasure via Feature Ablation Is Fully Reversible

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible with a gap: non-reversible feature consumption is theoretically interesting but the direct safety implication is more about refining our mental model of computation than a practical intervention.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires ablating features at one layer, running forward to a later layer, then patching back. This multi-layer intervention pipeline is advanced for beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: 15 features with ablate-and-reinsert experiments at specific layers. Sustained effort but well-defined protocol.

novelty.reasoning: While concept erasure with SAEs has been studied, the specific question of whether ablation at one layer can be 'undone' by reinserting the feature at a later layer (reversibility testing) is not directly addressed in existing work. The multi-layer ablate-and-reinsert protocol represents a novel experimental design. The closest work focuses on erasure effectiveness rather than reversibility.

evidence.source: Evaluating SAEs on Targeted Concept Erasure Tasks (arXiv 2411.18895, 2024)
evidence.finding: Evaluates SAEs on concept erasure tasks, but focuses on erasure effectiveness rather than reversibility of ablation.

evidence.source: Use Sparse Autoencoders to Discover Unknown Concepts, Not to Act on Known Concepts (arXiv 2506.23845, 2025)
evidence.finding: Argues SAE features are better for discovery than intervention, implicitly questioning the reliability of feature-based concept erasure.
Compares transcoders and SAEs for steering, but does not study reversibility of feature ablation across layers.
